newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ifo-German growth to gain pace but EMU poses risks.
newsitem.headline: Ifo-German growth to gain pace but EMU poses risks.

text.p: Germany faces an acceleration of economic growth alongside moderate inflation through 1998 but doubts about Europe's planned monetary union may yet kill off the recovery, the Ifo research institute said.

In its half-yearly report published on Tuesday, Ifo forecast that Europe's largest economy will grow 2.25 percent on average in 1997 and 2.5 to three percent in 1998, mainly because the weak mark and global trade growth are boosting exports.

Consumer inflation should stay weak, averaging 1.75 percent in 1997 and rising to two percent in 1998. Unemployment has peaked and should come down slowly in west Germany but is set to keep rising in east Germany, Ifo added.

German gross domestic product (GDP) grew by more than two percent year-on-year in the first half of 1997, with capacity utilisation rising in a manufacturing sector buoyed by an export boom, but falling in the construction sector.
"Seen overall, the conditions for a continuation of the economic upturn are good but there are substantial risks, particularly in connection with the planned European monetary union," Ifo said.

Fears that the single currency, or euro, will be soft could cause a further weakening of the mark while expectations of a delay of the euro's launch could have the opposite effect, causing the mark to surge, Ifo said.
The former scenario would hurt the economy by forcing the Bundesbank and other European central banks to raise interest rates to stave off imported inflation, it said.
The latter possibility would choke off the export growth that has been the driving force behind Germany's recovery.

Ifo said it was basing its forecasts on the assumption that world trade will grow between seven and eight percent in 1997 and 1998 and that monetary conditions will stay favourable, with the mark not weakening further and the Bundesbank raising interest rates only slightly through 1998.
But Ifo conceded the forecast of a steady mark was risky.

"There could be a further sharp mark depreciation if the confidence in the mark and the other European currencies is weakened further in connection with the debate about the Maastricht criteria," it said.
"The Bundesbank and the other European central banks could then see themselves forced to raise interest rates significantly in order to preempt the danger of inflation."

Ifo also said it would be highly regrettable if the government's planned tax reform foundered and warned it would be "fatal" if the zeal for structural reform waned at a time when economic conditions for such reforms are favourable.
The Bonn government has vowed to press ahead with its tax reform plans which envisage 30 billion marks in tax cuts, even if it takes until the turn of the century.

The failure to implement the reform has cast doubt on the country's ability to remove structural rigidities, such as inflexible labour markets, that have gnawed away at the competitiveness of German industry and kept unemployment high.
The reform has been blocked by the opposition Social Democrats who hold a majority in the upper house of parliament.

Ifo said domestic capital spending and private consumption will contribute to growth next year but the continuing recession in the construction sector will restrain the breadth and force of the recovery.
Real exports of physical goods will rise by nine percent on average in 1997 and by just under seven percent in 1998, with the weak mark contributing about one third to export growth in 1997.
Meanwhile the impact of the mark's weakness on inflation is being curbed by tight competition which is preventing companies from passing import price gains onto the consumer, Ifo said.
West Germany's labour market is experiencing its first improvement since the recession of 1992/1993, Ifo said.
The upturn has come so late in the recovery because companies were bent on rationalising and raising productivity early on in the recovery.
The decline in employment in the region's manufacturing sector is slowing down while some export-oriented sectors like the car sector are planning to hire more workers.

With employment in the service sector set to keep rising, overall employment in east Germany will no longer decline in the second half of 1997 and should rise slightly, by 140,000 or 0.5 percent in 1998.

Ifo predicted more than three million people would be out of work on average in west Germany in 1997, up from 2.8 million in 1996. That gives a projected unemployment rate of 9.8 percent after 9.0 percent. The forecast for 1998 is just under 2.9 million, a rate of 9.3 percent.

In east Germany, particularly hard hit by the building recession, unemployment should rise by 150,000 to 1.3 million people in 1997, a rate of 17.7 percent, increasing to about 1.35 million people or 18.4 percent in 1998, Ifo said.

Overall, Ifo forecasts pan-German unemployment will average 4.3 million people or 11.3 percent in 1997, up from just below four million or 10.3 percent in 1996. It expects unemployment to fall to 4.26 million people or 11.1 percent in 1998.
Ifo said rising exports had boosted capacity production in German industry to levels last seen in boom phases at the start of the 1970s and late 80s/early 90s.
By contrast, domestic demand was not stimulating growth and private consumer spending was growing only moderately. Ifo predicted consumer spending would rise by two percent in real terms in 1998.
"The split economy in the sense of a relatively weak domestic economy alongside a strong export sector should continue for a while," Ifo said.
But domestic demand should increase through 1998 as corporate earnings rise and capacity utilisation increases, causing a rise in investment.
